q: What is attention in neural networks?
short: A mechanism that computes a weighted sum of values, with weights from a softmax over query–key similarity scores, so the model focuses on the relevant inputs.
detail: c = Σ softmax(score(q, kᵢ)) vᵢ; differentiable, learned end to end.
mistakes: Describing it as a hard selection.

q: What is the bottleneck problem in encoder–decoder RNNs?
short: The entire input must be compressed into one fixed-size context vector; information about early tokens is lost on long inputs and all parts are weighted equally.
detail: Quality drops beyond ≈30 tokens (Sutskever et al.).

q: Explain queries, keys and values.
short: The query is what we're looking for, keys are what each item offers for matching, values are the content returned. Scores compare the query with keys; weights mix the values.
detail: In self-attention all three are linear projections of the same inputs.
mistakes: Assuming keys and values must be identical.

q: What is scaled dot-product attention?
short: softmax(QKᵀ/√d_k)V: dot-product scores scaled by √d_k, softmax over keys, then a weighted sum of values.
detail: Transformer default; one matrix multiply.

q: Self-attention vs cross-attention?
short: Self: Q, K, V from the same sequence (relations within it). Cross: Q from one sequence, K and V from another (alignment between them).
detail: Transformer decoders use both.

q: What is causal (masked) attention?
short: Attention where position i can only attend to positions ≤ i, implemented by adding −∞ to future scores before softmax.
detail: Enables parallel training of autoregressive models without leakage.

q: Why does a Transformer need positional encoding?
short: Self-attention is permutation-equivariant: without position information the model can't tell word order.
detail: Learned or sinusoidal encodings are added to embeddings; RoPE/ALiBi are modern alternatives.
mistakes: Saying attention weights encode position automatically.

q: What is multi-head attention?
short: Several attention operations in parallel with different learned projections; outputs concatenated and projected by W_O, letting heads capture different relationships.
detail: h = 8, d_k = 64 for d_model = 512.
follow: Does it multiply the cost by h?
mistakes: Thinking each head uses the full dimension.

q: Teacher forcing vs free running?
short: Teacher forcing feeds ground-truth previous tokens during training; free running feeds the model's own predictions at inference, causing exposure bias.
detail: Mitigations: scheduled sampling, beam search.
mistakes: Using teacher forcing at test time.

q: What does the softmax in attention guarantee?
short: Non-negative weights summing to 1, so the output is a convex combination of the values, and everything stays differentiable.
detail: Temperature controls sharpness.
follow: What happens with very large scores?

q: Why scale by √d_k? Derive it.
short: If q and k have i.i.d. components with mean 0, variance 1, Var(qᵀk) = Σ Var(q_j k_j) = d_k. Dividing by √d_k restores unit variance, keeping softmax out of saturation.
detail: Saturated softmax has gradients ≈ 0.
mistakes: Saying it's for numerical overflow only.

q: q = (0.8, 0.6); keys (0.5, 0.3), (0.9, 0.7), (0.4, 0.2). Compute the attention weights.
detail: The slide's (0.21, 0.62, 0.17) is wrong.

q: Additive vs dot-product attention?
short: Additive: vᵀtanh(W_q q + W_k k), parameters, handles d_q ≠ d_k, O(dh) per pair. Dot-product: no parameters, needs equal sizes, one matrix multiply, much faster on GPUs.
detail: Scaled dot-product matches additive quality at large d.

q: Walk through one Bahdanau decoder step.
short: Score every encoder state against s_{t−1}: e_{t,i} = vᵀtanh(W_s s_{t−1} + W_h h_i); α = softmax(e); c_t = Σ α h_i; s_t = RNN([y_{t−1}; c_t], s_{t−1}); P(y_t) = softmax(W_o[s_t; c_t]).
detail: Bidirectional encoder gives h_i both contexts.

q: Self-attention vs RNN vs CNN: path length and cost?
short: Self-attention: O(1) path, O(n²d) per layer, fully parallel. RNN: O(n) path, O(nd²), sequential. CNN: O(log n) with dilation, O(knd²), parallel.
detail: Attention is cheaper than RNN when n < d.
follow: How do efficient Transformers cut the n²?
mistakes: Saying attention is linear in n.

q: Is self-attention permutation-invariant?
short: Equivariant: Attention(PX) = P·Attention(X). Each token's output doesn't depend on order, so order must be injected via positional encodings.
detail: Pooled outputs are invariant.
follow: Do causal masks add order information?

q: Why do sinusoidal encodings help with relative position?
short: For each frequency, PE(pos + k) is PE(pos) rotated by angle kω_i, a linear map independent of pos, and PE(p)·PE(p+k) depends only on k.
detail: RoPE applies this rotation directly to Q and K.
example: '3 positions back' looks the same everywhere.
follow: Why can learned embeddings fail to extrapolate?

q: Implement causal scaled dot-product attention in NumPy.
short: S = Q @ K.T / sqrt(dk); S[np.triu_indices(n, 1)] = -inf; A = softmax(S, axis=-1); return A @ V.
detail: Subtract the row max before exp.

q: How do efficient attention variants reduce the O(n²) cost?
short: Sparsity (local/sliding windows, strided, block-sparse), low-rank or kernel approximations (Linformer, Performer), memory-efficient exact kernels (FlashAttention: tiling, no n×n materialisation), and retrieval/compression of past context.
detail: FlashAttention keeps exact attention but cuts memory traffic.

q: Do attention weights explain predictions?
short: Only partially. Weights show information flow at one layer; residual connections, multiple heads/layers and value vectors matter too, and alternative weight patterns can produce the same output.
detail: Use attribution methods (integrated gradients, attention rollout) cautiously.

q: Design attention for forecasting hourly network traffic with daily and weekly cycles.
short: Causal self-attention over past windows with positional/time-of-day embeddings, multiple heads to capture daily (24 h) and weekly (168 h) lags, cross-attention to calendar/event covariates, MSE/quantile loss, chronological validation.
detail: Watch O(n²) cost for long windows; consider patching.

q: Derive the gradient of attention output w.r.t. the scores.
short: c = Σ α_i v_i, α = softmax(e). ∂c/∂e_j = α_j(v_j − c): increasing a score pulls the output towards that value relative to the current mix.
detail: Softmax Jacobian α_i(δ_ij − α_j).
example: If v_j = c the gradient is zero.
follow: What happens when α is one-hot?

q: Learned vs sinusoidal vs rotary positional encodings?
short: Learned: flexible, no extrapolation. Sinusoidal: fixed, extrapolates in principle, relative offsets linear. RoPE: rotates Q and K by position so scores depend on relative offset; widely used in modern LLMs; ALiBi adds a distance penalty.
detail: Context-length extension tricks scale RoPE frequencies.
example: BERT learned; original Transformer sinusoidal; LLaMA RoPE.
follow: Why does RoPE give relative-position scores?

q: What is exposure bias, and how do attention models mitigate it?
short: Mismatch between training on gold prefixes and generating from own outputs; errors compound. Mitigations: scheduled sampling, beam search, sequence-level objectives (minimum risk, RL), data noising.
detail: Large LMs mitigate it partly through scale and sampling strategies.
example: Translation drifting after a wrong word.
follow: Why not just drop teacher forcing?
